newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-France to reveal Dassault merger plan in Jan.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-France to reveal Dassault merger plan in Jan.

text.p: The French government will announce in early January plans for merging state-owned aircraft group Aerospatiale with warplane maker Dassault Aviation, a defence department official said on Friday.
"We're on track with the timetable," the official said. "We should be able to make an announcement in early January on how the merger between the two will be carried out."
The official said talks were progressing well on the linkup to create a single large air and defence company aimed at rivalling heavyweight international competitors.
Combined, the two companies will be a similar size to Europe's two other big large aircraft makers, Daimler-Benz Aerospace (DASA) and British Aerospace.
Earlier, family-controlled Dassault Aviation said the two companies had made a joint proposal to the government outlining the organisational structure of the linkup.
"They deposited a draft (plan) for the government's approval that was sponsored jointly" by Aerospatiale chairman Yves Michot and Dassault Aviation boss Serge Dassault, a Dassault spokesman.
"The conversations (between Michot and Dassault) have gone well" and the government should be able "to announce something interesting" in early January, the Dassault spokesman said.

Earlier Friday, newspaper Le Monde reported Defence Minister Charles Millon would announce the new group's structure early in the new year but talks were continuing with the state on financial aspects and valuation of the companies' assets.

Le Monde said Dassault Aviation would be held 100 percent by the merged group to be baptised Dassault-Aerospatiale. In the new entity, Dassault-Aviation would group combat and business plane activities and enjoy significant independence.

The three other divisions would be made up of Aerospatiale units -- civilian aircraft, space, defence and missile activities, and helicopters. The plan envisages creation of a new maintenance unit to group technical operations.
The plan submitted by the two groups leaves open the issue of whether the management structure will be single or two tier.

Under a two-tier scenario, Dassault, 71, could be chairman of the supervisory board while Aerospatiale chief Michot could head a board of directors made up of three representatives of the state-owned group and two representatives from Dassault.
Dassault's stake in the future group will hinge tax liabilities for the Dassault families and on valuation of the two companies' assets which still is under way, Le Monde said.
Aerospatiale has nearly five times Dassault's turnover but last year Aerospatiale had a net loss of nearly one billion francs compared with Dassault's net profit of 526 million.
The merger was strongly opposed by Dassault who wanted to keep his family firm's independence but he later backed down.

The government has said the new company should be set up so that its capital can be opened to others as soon as possible. The merger would be the first step toward privatising Aerospatiale which is on the government's selloff list.

Earlier this week, Industry Minister Franck Borotra told the two companies to step up their merger efforts to meet the challenge posed by the linkup of Boeing-McDonnell Douglas creating the world's biggest aerospace company.

The government gave the two companies until year end to seal details of their merger. But Aerospatiale said last summer it thought legal formalities would drag out the process and the new company would not start up until mid-1997 at the earliest.
